titel: Legal form of funds and ETFs
kurz: How the management and custody of a fund are divided, which rules apply to retail funds, and why a pure gold product cannot be a UCITS.

bloecke.md:
A portfolio might, for example, contain a world ETF, a gold ETC and a crypto ETN. All three have an ISIN, can be bought via Xetra and have a price history. Legally, they are three different products. The difference only has an effect if the provider fails.

Under the German Investment Code (KAGB), a German fund is usually a pool of assets without legal personality of its own, looked after by two separate companies. Funds from other EU states such as Ireland or Luxembourg are sometimes set up as companies with their own legal personality. Even then, the fund assets are separate from the assets of the management company. A fund thus differs both from a stake in a company and from a claim against a debtor.

## Management and custody

The **fund management company** (KVG) makes the investment decisions, calculates the unit value and is responsible for distribution. Until the KAGB reform of 2013 it was called a Kapitalanlagegesellschaft (investment company), which is why the abbreviation “KAG” is still often seen. The KVG does not own the fund assets. They are held by the [[Depositary|depositary]], a legally independent credit institution. The depositary holds the securities in custody, issues units and redeems them. It also checks whether the KVG calculates unit prices correctly, complies with the investment limits and uses the income properly.

This separation is laid down by law and forms the basis of the structure. In a German fund, the fund assets constitute [[Segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen)|segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen)]]. They belong economically to the unitholders, do not appear on the KVG's balance sheet and do not become part of the insolvency estate if the KVG becomes insolvent. If the KVG becomes unable to pay its debts, the right to manage the fund passes to the depositary. The depositary winds up the fund or transfers it to another company. This does not involve a forced sale at rock-bottom prices.

- The investor is the economic co-owner of the segregated fund assets and thus has a proportionate interest in everything the fund holds.
- The KVG manages the assets, makes the investment decisions and does the accounting. It does not own the assets itself.
- The depositary holds the securities, issues units and monitors the KVG.
- The investor's custodian bank only holds the fund units. Its insolvency does not affect the holding, because securities in the securities account are the customer's property and are separated from the estate in insolvency.

Statutory deposit protection of €100,000 per customer and institution does not concern any of these levels. It only covers balances, that is, the settlement account, and at a bank also outstanding monetary claims from securities transactions. If an institution cannot return securities held in custody, or if an investment firm owes money from securities transactions, statutory investor compensation applies, but only at 90% and up to a maximum of €20,000. For banks, it is provided by the relevant deposit guarantee scheme (for private banks, the compensation scheme of German banks, Entschädigungseinrichtung deutscher Banken), and for investment firms by the compensation scheme for securities trading firms (Entschädigungseinrichtung der Wertpapierhandelsunternehmen).

## Investment rules for UCITS

Not every fund may be sold to private investors. The European directive on undertakings for collective investment in transferable securities (UCITS; in German [[UCITS (OGAW)|OGAW]]) lays down what such a retail fund may hold. The abbreviation UCITS in the fund name is a binding assurance that the fund complies with a verified set of rules. These include diversification, a regular right of redemption (in Germany at least twice a month by law, daily is usual), restrictions on derivatives and ongoing supervision by BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority) or another EU authority.

The best-known provision is the 5/10/40 rule of Section 206 KAGB. A more generous exception applies to index funds, because otherwise an index could not be replicated. Under Section 209 KAGB, an index UCITS may hold up to 20% per issuer, and up to 35% in the case of a single issuer. The precondition is that the index is sufficiently diversified, appropriately published and recognised by the supervisory authority.

bloecke.md: These rules explain many product decisions on the European market. A UCITS must diversify and may not invest directly in commodities. A product that tracks only a single asset such as gold, oil or bitcoin therefore cannot be a UCITS. For private investors in the EU, a different wrapper is needed, and this is usually a debt security.

bloecke.md:
## Open-ended and closed-ended funds

In an open-ended fund, the number of units is variable. When money flows in, new units are created, and when units are redeemed, they are cancelled. The price is the net asset value, that is, the fund assets divided by the number of units. An investor does not have to look for a buyer, because the fund itself redeems the units.

A closed-ended fund raises a fixed sum and accepts no further money after that. Such funds finance a specific asset such as a ship, a wind farm or a property. Legally, they are usually an entrepreneurial participation, often as a GmbH & Co. KG (a German limited partnership). There is no right of redemption, only a fixed term of often ten years or more and a thin secondary market with discounts. A total loss is possible. These characteristics cannot be recognised from the word “fund” in the prospectus.

Open-ended real estate funds lie in between. They are formally open-ended, but have a statutory minimum holding period and a notice period, because a building cannot be sold on the same day (details in module 18).

bloecke.md:
## ETF as a way of trading

The abbreviation ETF only indicates the route by which you acquire the unit. With a traditional fund, purchase and redemption go directly through the fund, once a day at a price that is only fixed after the close of trading. With an exchange-traded index fund, investors buy and sell continuously on the stock exchange, at prices quoted by market makers. As a rule, only authorised trading firms can subscribe for or redeem units directly with the fund.

The abbreviation says nothing about the content of the fund. There are index funds that are not traded on the stock exchange, and exchange-traded funds with active management. The assets of these active ETFs are growing quickly in Europe, from €52.5 billion at the end of 2024 to around €108 billion at the end of June 2026. Measured against the total assets of European ETFs and ETCs of around €3.2 trillion, that is around 3.4%. Active ETFs are thus a niche, albeit the fastest-growing one. Equating “ETF” with “passive, broad, cheap” will therefore be wrong more often in future.

bloecke.md:
## Issue and redemption of ETF units

An investor who buys 100 ETF units on the stock exchange acquires them from a market maker and not from the fund company. If the market maker's inventory is not sufficient, a so-called authorised participant steps in. It buys the index basket on the stock market, delivers it to the fund and receives new units in return. This process is called creation. In the reverse process, redemption, it returns units and receives the basket in exchange.

This exchange keeps the market price close to the value of the fund assets. If the price were significantly higher, the authorised participant could buy a basket cheaply, sell the units received for it at a higher price on the stock exchange and keep the difference as profit. These transactions make the price difference disappear. The ongoing reference value is the [[iNAV]], an indicative net asset value that is recalculated every 15 to 60 seconds during trading hours.

Fund size therefore says little about tradability, even if this is surprising at first. Tradability depends above all on how liquid the securities in the basket are and how many market makers provide quotes. A small ETF on highly liquid blue chips often has a narrower bid-ask spread than a large ETF on niche securities.

bloecke.unter: As a rule, the investor does not deal directly with the fund. The detour via the share basket ensures that the market price and the unit value stay close together.

bloecke.md:
## ETF, ETC, ETN

The three product types are traded on the stock exchange in the same way and often come from the same provider. Only the ETF is a fund.

An ETC tracks a single commodity and is legally a [[Bearer bond (Inhaberschuldverschreibung)|bearer bond (Inhaberschuldverschreibung)]]. Such a product is not possible as a UCITS, because a single commodity violates the diversification requirement. Reputable gold ETCs are backed by physically stored metal, some with a right to delivery. This security is based on the collateral agreement; fund law does not apply to ETCs.

An ETN has the same legal form but does not track a commodity. It is a debt security on an index, a currency or a crypto asset. Some ETNs are collateralised, others are not. If the issuer defaults, the investor is an ordinary creditor and receives a pro rata distribution, regardless of where the tracked index currently stands. German investors had this experience in 2008 with certificates from Lehman Brothers, which were structured in the same way legally.

bloecke.md:
An index ETF and an index certificate on the same index can move in lockstep for years. They differ only in their legal form. With the fund, the assets remain intact even if the provider disappears. With the debt security, they are lost along with the provider.

Before buying, you can check the legal form in three places: the abbreviation in the product name (UCITS ETF, ETC, ETN, certificate), the key information document under the heading for the type of product, and whether a fund domicile is stated. A fund has a fund domicile; a debt security has an issuer instead.

Providers close products that do not pay off for them. As an industry rule of thumb, a fund size of about €50 million to €100 million is regarded as the lower limit for economic operation. Unlike in a default, in a liquidation the fund's securities are sold, and investors receive their share of the net asset value.

The drawback is the tax effect. The liquidation counts as a sale. Accumulated gains become taxable, and the tax deferred until then falls due at a time the investor did not choose. Fund size and the age of a fund are therefore selection criteria, even though they have nothing to do with the investment strategy.

## Limits of the legal form

The segregated fund assets protect against the failure of the management company. They do not protect against falling prices, a badly constructed index, excessive costs or your own decision to sell at the bottom. Protection against insolvency says nothing about the quality of the securities a fund holds.

Conversely, issuer risk does not mean a certain loss. A collateralised gold ETC from a large issuer has an additional layer of risk that you need to know about and price in, but that does not make it a high-risk security. Instead of classifying products as good or bad, you should check which risks a product brings in addition to market risk and whether the investor is compensated for them.

mitnehmen: A German fund is usually a pool of segregated fund assets without legal personality of its own, which the KVG manages, the depositary holds in custody and which economically belongs to the investors. Foreign funds are sometimes companies, and their assets are also kept separate from the assets of the management company.

UCITS (OGAW) is a set of rules for diversification, redemption and derivatives; in the KAGB, the diversification rules are in Sections 206 and 209, redemption in Section 98 and the derivatives rules in Section 197 and the Derivatives Ordinance (DerivateV). The set of rules says nothing about returns.
Because a UCITS must diversify, a product on a single commodity cannot be a UCITS, and that is why ETCs and ETNs exist as debt securities.
ETF describes the way of trading and says nothing about the investment strategy; there are also active ETFs, and their assets are growing quickly in Europe.
Open-ended and closed-ended funds differ fundamentally, because a closed-ended fund has no right of redemption and a total loss is possible.

begriffe.text: Assets of a German contractual investment fund (Section 1(10) KAGB) that are legally separate from the assets of the management company and do not become part of the insolvency estate if it becomes insolvent. They belong economically to the unitholders.

Legally independent credit institution that holds the fund assets in custody, issues and redeems units and monitors the management company. If the management company becomes insolvent, the depositary takes over the management of the fund.

German abbreviation (Organismus für gemeinsame Anlagen in Wertpapieren) for UCITS, undertakings for collective investment in transferable securities. The EU set of rules for retail funds contains requirements on diversification, redemption, derivatives and supervision, and is implemented in Germany in the German Investment Code (KAGB).
Indicative net asset value of an ETF, calculated every 15 to 60 seconds during trading hours. Market makers use it as a guide when providing binding bid and ask prices.

Security that embodies a claim against the issuer. The holder is a creditor and, if the issuer becomes insolvent, only receives the pro rata distribution from the insolvency estate. ETCs, ETNs and certificates have this legal form.
